werk/branford-marsalis-royal-garden-blue.text:
Royal Garden Blues was released in 1986 and is an album by saxophonist Branford Marsalis. His brother Delfeayo produced. Ron Carter and Herbie Hancock played on it, and Ellis Marsalis is at the piano on Swingin' at the Haven, which he wrote himself. The Wrath of Tain is a tribute to drummer Jeff Tain Watts. The title song is an arrangement of a jazz standard, and Spike Lee directed the video.

The album was nominated for a Grammy. One newspaper heard the influence of Miles Davis's mid-sixties quintet. Reviews were divided: some found it conservatively played, others called it playful. AllMusic saw it as one of the saxophonist's more playful records.
werk/branford-marsalis-royal-garden-blue.listen: Listen to Royal Garden Blues and notice the saxophone's improvisation above the accompaniment.

werk/branford-marsalis-scenes-in-the-cit.text:
Scenes in the City, from 1984, was saxophonist Branford Marsalis's first album under his own name. In 1982 he had already recorded Fathers and Sons, together with his father and brothers. Thomas Mowrey produced the record. Bassist Ron Carter plays on three tracks and the line-up closely resembles that of his brother Wynton's albums from the same period. Marsalis wrote three pieces himself, and the pianists Mulgrew Miller and Kenny Kirkland contributed one each. The title piece was composed twenty years earlier by Charles Mingus.

The album received four out of four stars in The Penguin Guide to Jazz and is included in that book's list of the thousand best jazz albums, as the only Marsalis record. Scott Yanow called it ambitious and consistently successful, an impressive start to a remarkable career.
werk/branford-marsalis-scenes-in-the-cit.listen: Listen to Scenes In the City and notice the narrator and how the saxophone responds to him.

werk/brian-eno-after-the-heat.text:
After the Heat was released in 1978 under the name Eno Moebius Roedelius. Brian Eno worked here for the second time with Dieter Moebius and Hans-Joachim Roedelius of Cluster, after Cluster & Eno in 1977. Once again the influential Krautrock producer Conny Plank was involved as engineer.

A number of piano-led instrumentals recall the earlier album, but according to Pitchfork, After the Heat lives in a world of its own. Trouser Press heard an alluring collection of instrumentals that cleverly sidesteps the pitfalls of ambient. There is also singing: in Broken Head the declaimed voice stands out through tape flanging, and Tzima N'Arki contains a vocal part recorded backwards with a snatch of the chorus of King's Lead Hat. That makes it not a pure ambient record.
werk/brian-eno-after-the-heat.listen: In Broken Head, listen to the declaimed voice and notice the floating effect that the tape flanging gives it.

werk/brian-eno-ambient-1-music-for-airpo.text:
After a long wait at Cologne Bonn airport, irritated by the atmosphere, Brian Eno conceived music made especially for airports. He began it during the production of David Bowie's Low in Berlin, where he recorded individual notes sung by three German women. Back in England he recorded Fred Frith on guitar and Robert Wyatt on piano. From all the recordings he made tape loops of different lengths, which run over one another.

The album was released in February 1979 and consists of four pieces. Eno wanted to bring calm and room for thought, with music that is as easy to ignore as it is interesting. It was his first record under the label ambient, and is seen as the record that spread the term. In 2016 Pitchfork called it the best ambient record ever.
werk/brian-eno-ambient-1-music-for-airpo.listen: Listen to 1/1 and notice the piano sounds that surface irregularly and without a fixed pulse. This is the only piece with a melody.

werk/brian-eno-another-green-world.text:
This third solo album by Brian Eno was recorded in July and August 1975 at Island Studios in London. He went into the studio without having written or prepared anything, and the first four days yielded nothing. He then sought support in his Oblique Strategies, cards with instructions meant to lead to new ideas. Guest musicians such as Robert Fripp, Phil Collins and John Cale played on it, but on seven tracks he plays everything himself.

The record forms a transition from his rock songs to the ambient work of the late seventies. Only five of the fourteen tracks have vocals. The instrumental pieces are melodic and rhythmic, and have titles such as In Dark Trees and The Big Ship. On St. Elmo's Fire, Fripp improvised a fast guitar solo, meant as an imitation of an electrical charge. The record charted almost nowhere in 1975, but was reviewed favourably and later appears on lists of the best albums of the seventies.
werk/brian-eno-another-green-world.listen: Listen to St. Elmo's Fire and notice the fast, sharp guitar solo, which is meant to imitate an electrical discharge.

werk/brian-eno-discreet-music.text:
Discreet Music came about after Brian Eno, lying in bed following a car accident, was left a record of eighteenth-century harp music by a friend. The music sounded almost inaudibly quiet, and Eno realised that music can also be part of the environment. The album leans on Erik Satie's idea of furniture music and on generative composition: few plans, little intervention.

The title piece lasts thirty minutes. A synthesizer with built-in memory plays two melodic phrases of different lengths, which shift over one another via an echo unit and two tape recorders. On the second half, studio musicians of the Cockpit Ensemble, conducted by Gavin Bryars, perform three variations on Pachelbel's Canon in D. The album is regarded as a clear step towards the ambient music that Eno would later define.
werk/brian-eno-discreet-music.listen: Listen to the first minutes of Discreet Music and notice how the same short phrases keep returning at a slightly different moment.

werk/brian-eno-here-come-the-warm-jets.text:
After leaving Roxy Music, Eno recorded his first solo album in twelve days in September 1973 at Majestic Studios in London. He invited sixteen guest musicians, including former bandmates and members of Hawkwind, Matching Mole and King Crimson, precisely because he thought they were musically incompatible. He wanted to see what happened when such different personalities worked against one another, and he directed them with body language and dance. He then processed the recordings so deeply that some tracks barely resemble what the musicians played.

The sound has been described as glam art pop. Cindy Tells Me, for example, contains tinkling pianos and fifties-style falsetto choruses, and Blank Frank borrows its drum rhythm from Bo Diddley. The lyrics are macabre but humorous and virtually without fixed meaning. The album was released in February 1974 and received mostly positive reviews. The title refers to a guitar that sounded like a jet engine being tuned.
werk/brian-eno-here-come-the-warm-jets.listen: In Blank Frank, listen to the drum rhythm, which is taken from a Bo Diddley song, and to how Eno builds an atmosphere of his own around it.

werk/brian-eno-music-for-films.text:
Brian Eno conceived this album as music for films that did not yet exist. In 1976 a version was released in an edition of five hundred copies, intended for filmmakers who wanted to use excerpts from it. The 1978 release was expanded with pieces from the years 1975 to 1978 and remained intended as a soundtrack for imagined films.

The tracks are short, from a minute and a half to just over four minutes. That differs from the long, drawn-out ambient pieces that came afterwards. Besides synthesizers and found sounds, other musicians play ordinary studio instruments, including Robert Fripp, Fred Frith, John Cale and Phil Collins. The method resembles that of David Bowie's album Low from 1977. Fragments of the album ended up in at least six real films.
werk/brian-eno-music-for-films.listen: Listen to Two Rapid Formations and notice how short the piece is and how quickly an atmosphere is established. Try to imagine a film image to go with it.

werk/brian-eno-taking-tiger-mountain-by-.text:
For his second solo album, Eno worked differently from on the debut. Instead of sixteen guests he used a regular core of five musicians: himself, Phil Manzanera, Brian Turrington, Freddie Smith and Robert Wyatt. The title comes from postcards of a Chinese revolutionary opera. To help the musicians along, Eno made cards with instructions together with Peter Schmidt, the Oblique Strategies, which during the recording determined what happened next.

The record is a loose concept album about espionage and the Chinese revolution, with lyrics that Eno made from nonsense syllables. The sound is calmer than on the debut, the themes are darker and the lyrics often humorous. Burning Airlines Give You So Much More was inspired by a plane crash near Paris in 1974. Phil Collins plays additional drums on Mother Whale Eyeless. The record did not chart, but received positive reviews and later attracted more attention.
werk/brian-eno-taking-tiger-mountain-by-.listen: In Burning Airlines Give You So Much More, listen to the lyrics with their quick rhymes and the subject of the plane crash.

werk/brian-wilson-i-just-wasn-t-made-for.text:
I Just Wasn't Made for These Times was Brian Wilson's second solo album and was released on 15 August 1995 on MCA Records. It is the soundtrack to a documentary of the same name by Don Was. Almost all the tracks are new recordings of old work by Wilson. The title comes from a song he wrote in 1966 with Tony Asher for The Beach Boys' Pet Sounds.

In 1995 Wilson said that at first he thought it would turn out contrived, because the songs had been heard so often. Then he understood the context and was able to speak freely, without worrying about what he said. He got the feeling that he mattered. The record includes Caroline, No, Love and Mercy and Do It Again, which he sings with his daughters Wendy and Carnie.
werk/brian-wilson-i-just-wasn-t-made-for.listen: Listen to Caroline, No and notice how vulnerable his voice sounds in this new recording of a song from 1966.

werk/brian-wilson-orange-crate-art.text:
In 1992 Van Dyke Parks asked the reclusive Brian Wilson to record an album together. He wanted to close off unfinished work and escape the weight of history surrounding their failed Smile project. Orange Crate Art was released in 1995 on Warner Bros. The title refers to the sunny, idealised paintings on wooden fruit crates, and the theme is a nostalgic picture of the history of California.

Although the album was announced as a collaboration, it consists mainly of songs that Parks wrote and arranged, with his dense wordplay and orchestrations. Wilson sang and made the vocal arrangements. Expectations were high, but the reviews were mixed and sales remained so low that the album did not chart. Parks said it took three years and 350,000 dollars and vanished without trace.
werk/brian-wilson-orange-crate-art.listen: Listen to Orange Crate Art and notice how the voice carries the lyric about oranges and the Californian dream image.

werk/britney-spears-baby-one-more-time.text:
Britney Spears appeared as a child in The All-New Mickey Mouse Club and afterwards sought a career as a teenage singer. A demo first brought her rejections, until Jive Records signed her in 1997. Producer Eric Foster White worked on her voice. From May 1998 she recorded half of the album at Cheiron Studios in Stockholm, with Max Martin and Rami Yacoub. Martin played her a song that had first been written for TLC. That group had turned it down.

The result is a mixture of pop, bubblegum pop and dance, with ballads such as From the Bottom of My Broken Heart and a cover of The Beat Goes On. Critics' first reactions were mixed: they praised the commercial feel, but also found it silly and premature. Later the record came to be seen as one of the most influential pop albums, with major consequences for pop culture.
werk/britney-spears-baby-one-more-time.listen: Listen to ...Baby One More Time and notice how the chorus sticks immediately. What does the melody do to achieve that?

werk/bruce-springsteen-born-to-run.text:
After the commercial disappointments of his first two albums, Springsteen was given one more chance by Columbia. He recorded at 914 Sound Studios in Blauvelt, New York, from January 1974, with the E Street Band, manager Mike Appel and later also Jon Landau as co-producer. He wanted to approach Phil Spector's Wall of Sound. He worked on the title track alone for six months. It ended up with 72 tracks, squeezed onto a sixteen-channel mixing desk. During the recording, Roy Bittan and Max Weinberg joined the band.

The songs are about people who feel trapped and dream of escape, with highways and travel as imagery. Singles were Born to Run and Tenth Avenue Freeze-Out. Critics praised the stories and the music, although some found the production too heavy. The album was the breakthrough and in 2003 was added to the National Recording Registry.
werk/bruce-springsteen-born-to-run.listen: In Born to Run, listen to the full, layered production. Try to hear how many instruments sound at once and which ones you can tell apart.

werk/bruce-springsteen-darkness-on-the-e.text:
After the breakthrough album Born to Run, Bruce Springsteen came into conflict with his manager Mike Appel. In July 1976 he brought a lawsuit, and as a result he could not work in the studio for almost a year. He toured with the E Street Band and wrote dozens of new songs along the way. A settlement followed on 28 May 1977. Four days later he began recording with Jon Landau at Atlantic Studios in New York, a process that later moved to the Record Plant.

Springsteen drew inspiration from the novels of John Steinbeck, the films of John Ford, punk and country. The Wall of Sound of its predecessor gave way to rawer hard rock in which the whole band counts. The characters are older than before and fight against overwhelming odds. The record reached number five in the United States and is later regarded as one of his best.
werk/bruce-springsteen-darkness-on-the-e.listen: Listen to Badlands and notice how the whole band plays as one block, rawer than the layered production of Born to Run.

werk/bruce-springsteen-greetings-from-as.text:
Bruce Springsteen recorded his debut from June to October 1972 at 914 Sound Studios in Blauvelt, New York. His first manager Mike Appel and Jim Cretecos produced the album in that cheap studio in order to save as much as possible of Columbia's advance. There was a row over the approach, and the compromise was a mix of five band tracks and five solo tracks. When label president Clive Davis rejected the album because it had no hit on it, Springsteen quickly wrote Blinded by the Light and Spirit in the Night. That is how the album came out in January 1973.

The singles did not chart and sales remained average, but the critics were positive. Lester Bangs praised the bold new writer with his overloaded lyrics and rhyme schemes. Others heard in the record the folk rock of Bob Dylan, combined with accessible melodies and elaborate arrangements. Rolling Stone later placed it on its list of the best debut albums.
werk/bruce-springsteen-greetings-from-as.listen: Listen to Spirit in the Night and notice the combination of piano and saxophone.

werk/bruce-springsteen-letter-to-you.text:
Bruce Springsteen was struggling with writer's block until, in April 2019, he wrote intensively for a week and a half. The death of George Theiss, an old bandmate, played a part. In November 2019 he recorded with the E Street Band in his own studio, in four days. Producers were Ron Aniello and himself. It was done live, without demos and with minimal overdubs. It was the first album with the band since High Hopes in 2014.

The lyrics are about regret, growing older and dying. Three songs he had already written before his 1973 debut: If I Was the Priest, Janey Needs a Shooter and Song for Orphans. He found old recordings when he was putting together a compilation album. Because of the pandemic the band could not tour, so the album was promoted with an online radio station and its own emoji. Critics responded with praise to its approach to ageing and death.
werk/bruce-springsteen-letter-to-you.listen: In Janey Needs A Shooter, listen to the band, which sounds live and raw. Bear in mind that this song dates from before Springsteen's 1973 debut.

werk/bruce-springsteen-nebraska.text:
After the great success of The River, Bruce Springsteen withdrew in September 1981 to a rented farmhouse in Colts Neck, New Jersey. There he read history and short stories, including Flannery O'Connor, and watched films. In his bedroom he recorded the songs on his own on a four-track recorder. He wanted to re-record them later with the E Street Band, but found those versions less good and released the recordings as they were. The album was released on 30 September 1982.

The sound is bare and sounds like a home recording. The songs tell of workers who fail again and again, and sometimes a perpetrator speaks, such as the murderer Charles Starkweather in the title song. Critics praised the bold choice and the personal tone. Later Nebraska came to be seen as one of the first home recordings by a major artist and had great influence on indie rock.
werk/bruce-springsteen-nebraska.listen: Listen to the title track Nebraska. Notice how little there is to hear: just a voice and a guitar, which brings the murderer's story close.

werk/bruce-springsteen-the-rising.text:
The Rising was released on 30 July 2002 and is Bruce Springsteen's twelfth studio album. It came seven years after The Ghost of Tom Joad, his longest gap between two studio albums, and was his first in almost twenty years with the E Street Band. It was also the start of a collaboration with producer Brendan O'Brien. After the attacks of 11 September 2001, a stranger said to him: "We need you now". The album draws largely on his thoughts about those days, although a few songs had been written earlier.

The title song tells of a firefighter going into the World Trade Center. My City of Ruins was originally about Asbury Park and took on a new meaning after the attacks. Worlds Apart is the most experimental track, with a strong Middle Eastern influence and qawwali singers in the intro. The reviews were mostly very positive, although some critics found the lyrics too vague. The album won two Grammys.
werk/bruce-springsteen-the-rising.listen: Listen to Worlds Apart and notice the intro: which voices do you hear there before the rock sound begins?

werk/bruce-springsteen-the-wild-the-inno.text:
That same year Bruce Springsteen had already released his debut, which was well received but sold little. For this second album he recorded with the E Street Band at 914 Sound Studios in Blauvelt, New York. The sessions ran from May to 23 September 1973. At the end two more songs were added, Rosalita (Come Out Tonight) and the new Incident on 57th Street, which were recorded from scratch. The album was released in November 1973, with virtually no advertising or launch.

The music leaves the folk influences of the debut behind and sounds like a mixture of nostalgic rock 'n' roll and soulful R&B, with long, vivid songs. It initially sold poorly, but critics were full of praise, and in the region around New York Springsteen became a local phenomenon. Until 1985, Rosalita was the song with which the band most often closed its concerts. After Born to Run, several songs grew into favourites on radio and in concert.
werk/bruce-springsteen-the-wild-the-inno.listen: In Rosalita (Come Out Tonight), listen to how the band builds the song, and notice the energy a concert closer needs.

werk/bruce-springsteen-tunnel-of-love.text:
Tunnel of Love is Bruce Springsteen's eighth studio album and was released on 9 October 1987. Members of the E Street Band played on it from time to time, but Springsteen recorded most of it himself, often with drum machines and synthesizers. The record therefore does not officially count as an album by that band. The lyrics are about love going wrong, a consequence of changes in his private life, above all his faltering marriage. He wrote about the difficulty of adult love, not about stadium anthems for the working man.

The songs are mid-tempo ballads and pop-style anthems. Brilliant Disguise became one of his biggest hits, and Tunnel of Love, One Step Up, Tougher Than the Rest and Spare Parts were also released as singles. The title song won a Grammy. Critics praised the record for its honesty. Rolling Stone later placed it on its list of the hundred best albums of the eighties.
werk/bruce-springsteen-tunnel-of-love.listen: Listen to Brilliant Disguise and notice the lyric about the feeling that you can never fully know another person.

werk/bruce-springsteen-wrecking-ball.text:
Bruce Springsteen wrote almost all the songs in 2011. The exceptions were older songs: the title song dates from 2009 and was meant as a farewell to Giants Stadium, Land of Hope and Dreams dates from 1998 or 1999. The financial crisis of 2008 had convinced him that he also had to write about the people and forces behind the misery in America. Saxophonist Clarence Clemons, who died in June 2011, still plays on two tracks. Members of the E Street Band and the Sessions Band also took part, plus guitarist Tom Morello.

The record is angry and socially engaged. We Take Care of Our Own sets a patriotic chorus against references to the aftermath of Hurricane Katrina. Death to My Hometown targets the practices of bankers on Wall Street. Musically the album mixes rock bombast with folk, gospel, Irish rhythms and sometimes electronic percussion. Rolling Stone named it the best album of 2012.
werk/bruce-springsteen-wrecking-ball.listen: Listen to We Take Care of Our Own and notice how the chorus sounds patriotic while the verses show another side.

werk/bryan-adams-cuts-like-a-knife.text:
Cuts Like a Knife is Bryan Adams's third studio album. He made it together with Bob Clearmountain, at Little Mountain Sound Studios in Vancouver. Recording ran from 13 August to 20 October 1982. Clearmountain mixed the record in Quebec and New York. In January 1983 the album was released on A&M Records.

Three singles brought Adams great fame: Straight from the Heart, the title track and This Time. Straight from the Heart is a ballad written by Eric Kagna, to which Adams added the instrumental bridge. It was the last song to be recorded. The video for Cuts Like a Knife was shown heavily on MTV in 1983 and contributed to the success. The album reached number eight on the American chart, went triple platinum in Canada and platinum in the United States. Outside North America it only became successful after Reckless.
werk/bryan-adams-cuts-like-a-knife.listen: Listen to Straight from the Heart and notice the instrumental bridge, which Adams himself contributed to Eric Kagna's song.

werk/bryan-adams-reckless.text:
Reckless was released on 5 November 1984, the day Bryan Adams turned twenty-five. As with the previous record, he produced the album himself together with Bob Clearmountain. Heaven was the first song to be recorded. It had been written earlier for the film A Night in Heaven and at first seemed too light for the album. In March 1984 the sessions began in Vancouver, together with songwriting partner Jim Vallance.

By August nine songs were finished, but Adams was not satisfied. His manager asked: where is the rock? Adams and Vallance then re-recorded One Night Love Affair and Summer of '69 and wrote Kids Wanna Rock. Six singles reached the American top twenty, and the album ultimately went to number one. It was the first Canadian record to sell more than a million copies in its home country. Kerrang! chose it as album of the year for 1985, and it won a Juno Award.
werk/bryan-adams-reckless.listen: Listen to Summer of '69, a song that was re-recorded when the singer wanted more rock, and notice how solid it sounds.

werk/bts-dark-en-wild.text:
DARK&WILD is the first studio album by the South Korean group BTS and was released on 20 August 2014 on Big Hit Entertainment. It has fourteen tracks, with Danger as the title track and War of Hormone as the second single. Danger was recorded in an improvised studio in a garage in Los Angeles. Beforehand the label placed a countdown clock on the website and a trailer with contrasting images, and let Let Me Know, written and produced by Suga, be streamed for free.

The album is a continuation of the group's school trilogy and leads into the next series. The music combines grunge guitars with hip hop and connects with R&B and electronica. The lyrics are about growing up, youthful desires and impatience for love. The album reached number two in South Korea, number three on Billboard's World Albums chart in the United States and won a Bonsang at the Golden Disc Awards.
werk/bts-dark-en-wild.listen: Listen to Danger and notice how the hard guitars and the rap together create a tense atmosphere.

werk/bts-wake-up.text:
Wake Up was released on 24 December 2014 in Japan on Pony Canyon. It was the first Japanese studio album by the South Korean boy band BTS and the second album overall. Of the thirteen tracks, three are Japanese versions of Korean singles from the preceding months: No More Dream, Boy in Luv and Danger. In addition there are two new, originally Japanese songs, The Stars and Wake Up.

The three singles had already been released as CDs in Japan. The album entered the Oricon albums chart at number three, the highest position the group had reached there until then, and stayed in that chart for thirteen weeks. With more than 28,000 copies it became the group's best-selling album in Japan at that point. In February 2015 the first Japanese tour followed, taking in Chiba, Osaka, Nagoya and Fukuoka.
werk/bts-wake-up.listen: Listen to The Stars, one of the two new Japanese songs, and notice how this song sounds next to the Japanese versions of the Korean singles.

werk/bts-wings.text:
WINGS is BTS's second Korean and fourth studio album. It was released on 10 October 2016 on Big Hit Entertainment, with Blood Sweat & Tears as lead single. The concept is strongly influenced by Demian, Hermann Hesse's novel about growing up, and is about temptation and growth. For the first time as a major group effort, it contains seven solo tracks, which show the individual strength of each member.

Leader RM explained that the harder a temptation is to resist, the more it occupies you, and that this uncertainty is part of growing up. In Begin, Jungkook tells of his journey to Seoul and meeting the other members. MAMA is about J-Hope's childlike feelings for his mother, and Awake was the first time Jin co-wrote the music. 2! 3! was the first official fan song. The reviews were positive, and in Korea it was, according to Gaon, the best-selling album of 2016.
werk/bts-wings.listen: Listen to MAMA and notice how personal a solo song about J-Hope's childhood and his mother sounds.

werk/bts-youth.text:
Youth was released on 7 September 2016 on Pony Canyon as the second Japanese-language and third studio album by the South Korean group BTS. It has thirteen tracks, including Japanese versions of songs such as Run, Fire and I Need U. The album came out as a regular edition and as an edition with a DVD, which contains the Japanese versions of the music videos for I Need U and Run, along with the video for For You.

The album was a hit. On the day of release 44,547 copies were sold and it topped the daily Oricon chart. In the first full week 76,483 changed hands, and Youth debuted at number one on the weekly chart. Shortly afterwards it was certified gold by the Recording Industry Association of Japan, for 100,000 copies sold. In Oricon's year-end chart for 2016 it came forty-eighth.
werk/bts-youth.listen: Listen to RUN (Japanese Ver.) and notice how a song from Korea sounds in Japanese.

werk/bud-shank-barefoot-adventure.text:
This album contains the music for Barefoot Adventure, the surf film that Bruce Brown made in 1961. All the pieces were written by saxophonist Bud Shank himself. He played them with a small jazz combo and released them on the label Pacific Jazz.

The line-up has Carmell Jones on trumpet, Bob Cooper on tenor saxophone, Dennis Budimir on guitar, Gary Peacock on bass and Shelly Manne on drums. The leader himself plays alto saxophone and baritone saxophone. The titles, such as Jungle Cruise, How High the Makaha and Ala Moana, refer to beach and sea. AllMusic gave the album three stars.
werk/bud-shank-barefoot-adventure.listen: Listen to Dance of the Sea Monsters and notice how the horns and the rhythm section together create a cinematic atmosphere.

werk/bud-shank-i-ll-take-romance.text:
I'll Take Romance is an album by saxophonist Bud Shank, released on the label World Pacific. The record consists of eleven well-known standards, from Smoke Gets in Your Eyes and Deep Purple to Embraceable You and How Deep Is the Ocean. Shank plays alto saxophone and flute. Some of the tracks were recorded with a backing group of trumpet, horn, saxophones and guitar, the rest with valve trombonist Bob Brookmeyer and pianist Claude Williamson.

What makes this record special is found in Jason Ankeney's review on AllMusic. He heard an album far removed from the sometimes bloodless coolness of the West Coast school and instead warm, as the title promises. He called the string arrangements sweet but never sentimental, with a sensitivity that colours Shank's lyrical alto sax and flute without drowning them out.
werk/bud-shank-i-ll-take-romance.listen: Listen to Someone to Watch Over Me and notice how lyrically the alto saxophone sings the melody, without the accompaniment overwhelming it.

werk/bud-shank-plays-tenor.text:
In late 1957 alto saxophonist Bud Shank recorded an album for the label Pacific Jazz on which he plays tenor saxophone. He works with a small quartet: Claude Williamson on piano, Don Prell on bass and Chuck Flores on drums. The repertoire consists of well-known standards, including Thou Swell, Tenderly, Over the Rainbow, All the Things You Are and Body and Soul.

Switching to another instrument does not fundamentally change his sound and style. The eight tracks last between just over four and almost eight minutes, so there is plenty of room for soloing. According to the AllMusic reviewer, the tenor does give his lyrical solos more soul and depth.
werk/bud-shank-plays-tenor.listen: Listen to Body and Soul and notice the tone of the tenor saxophone: does it sound deeper and softer than you would expect from an alto saxophone?

werk/buddy-rich-buddy-rich-sings-johnny-.text:
In 1956 drummer Buddy Rich recorded an album on which he sang himself. It contains only songs for which Johnny Mercer wrote the lyrics. The composers vary from track to track: Harold Arlen supplies a good number, including Out of This World and One for My Baby, while Skylark is by Hoagy Carmichael. Buddy Bregman wrote the arrangements and conducted the orchestra.

It was the first of three vocal albums he recorded. The band includes trumpeter Harry Sweets Edison, tenor saxophonist Ted Nash and pianist Jimmy Rowles, among others. Alvin Stoller is also behind the drums, alongside the singer himself. The result is a record on which a well-known jazz drummer takes on the role of singer, in a series of familiar songs from the American repertoire.
werk/buddy-rich-buddy-rich-sings-johnny-.listen: Listen to Blues In The Night and notice how a drummer presents himself as a singer here and how Bregman's orchestra accompanies him.

werk/buddy-rich-this-one-s-for-basie.text:
Drummer Buddy Rich recorded this album as a tribute to bandleader Count Basie. He played with an eleven-piece orchestra, with trumpeters Pete Candoli and Harry Sweets Edison, trombonist Frank Rosolino, pianist Jimmy Rowles and guitarist Bill Pitman, among others. Marty Paich wrote the arrangements.

The repertoire consists of pieces associated with Basie, such as Blue and Sentimental, Jumpin' at the Woodside, Shorty George and 9:20 Special. Blues for Basie, by Edison, is at just over seven minutes the longest track. Verve later reissued the record. In the sixties it appeared under the title Big Band Shout, but without Blues for Basie.
werk/buddy-rich-this-one-s-for-basie.listen: Listen to Jumpin' at the Woodside and notice how the drummer and the small orchestra swing together.

werk/bugge-wesseltoft-it-s-snowing-on-my.text:
This was Bugge Wesseltoft's first solo piano record. He recorded it on 15 and 16 October 1997 at Rainbow Studio in Oslo. Siegfried Loch produced, and Jan Erik Kongshaug was at the controls as engineer.

The album contains traditional Christmas songs and a few pieces of the pianist's own, including the title song and Into eternal silence. The songs come from different languages: there are Norwegian, German, English and Latin titles. ACT Music released the record in 1997. In 2017 it was described as the label's best-selling album, with more than 150,000 copies. In Norway it reached number three in 2009, and since then it has returned to the charts around Christmas every year.
werk/bugge-wesseltoft-it-s-snowing-on-my.listen: In Stille Nacht, listen to how a familiar Christmas melody takes on a colour of its own with just a piano.

werk/burna-boy-african-giant.text:
Burna Boy recorded African Giant between August and November 2018 with producer Kel-P. They spent six weeks in a hotel room in Lagos and made twenty-three tracks. The title comes from his angry reaction to the organisers of Coachella over the small letters in which his name appeared on the poster. The album was released on 26 July 2019 and mixes Afrobeats, Afrobeat, dancehall, pop and hip hop. He called it his most personal record, with themes such as the political situation in Nigeria and violence in the region.

Anybody contains a sample of Angélique Kidjo. Dangote, partly in Yoruba and Nigerian pidgin, is an angry indictment of poverty in Nigeria, with horns in the style of Fela. Gum Body is a love duet with Jorja Smith. Critics called the record coherent and praised him for not diluting his sound. It received a Grammy nomination for Best World Music Album.
werk/burna-boy-african-giant.listen: Listen to Dangote and notice the jazzy, Fela-style horns that accompany the dancehall rhythm.

werk/burna-boy-on-a-spaceship.text:
On a Spaceship is the second studio album by the Nigerian singer and songwriter Burna Boy. It was released on 16 November 2015 on Spaceship Records and Universal Music Group. He worked with many producers, including Spellz, Sarz, Orbeat and J Fem, and invited guests such as Wizkid, Wande Coal, Phyno, Flavour and AKA.

The singles Soke, Jealousy, Rizzla, Duro Ni Be and The Realest were released spread across 2015 and 2016. Soke was nominated for best Afrobeat video at the Nigerian Music Video Awards. The reception was mixed. Critics praised tracks such as Soke, Rizzla and If People Must Die, but found the album too long and too safe. They also missed producer LeriQ, who had worked on his earlier output. One reviewer saw the record as an answer to the industry, which had passed over his earlier work.
werk/burna-boy-on-a-spaceship.listen: Listen to Soke and notice how the voice and the beat together carry the song.

werk/burna-boy-outside.text:
Outside is the third album by the Nigerian singer Burna Boy and follows his debut EP Redemption from 2016. He himself calls it a mixtape: a mixture of Afrobeats, dancehall, reggae and road rap, with guests such as J Hus, Lily Allen and Mabel. The album was released on 26 January 2018. He recorded the title song on Pete Townshend's studio boat, and Ye came about after a night out at a club in Lagos.

Producer Phantom made the beat in under two hours. When people searching for Kanye West's album Ye ended up at this song, the number of streams shot up. Critics praised the versatility, and Pulse Nigeria called it the best Nigerian record of 2018.
werk/burna-boy-outside.listen: Listen to Koni Baje and notice the talking drums and the bongos in this song inspired by jùjú.

werk/burna-boy-twice-as-tall.text:
Burna Boy recorded this album mainly in Ahoada in Nigeria, in the first months of the coronavirus pandemic in 2020. Diddy was executive producer together with Burna Boy's mother Bose Ogulu. Because of the lockdown they worked via Zoom and by exchanging files. Telz produced most of it, alongside Rexxie and Timbaland, among others. The sleeve shows the singer as a titan striding over modern roads and ancient monuments.

The album mixes Afrobeats, Afrobeat, dancehall, pop and hip hop. It opens with Level Up, featuring Youssou N'Dour. Alarm Clock leans on Fela Kuti and begins with a spoken intro by Diddy. Monsters You Made, with Chris Martin, is about injustice, slavery and prejudice. It ends with a spoken piece by the Ghanaian writer Ama Ata Aidoo. Twice as Tall won a Grammy for Best Global Music Album.
werk/burna-boy-twice-as-tall.listen: In Monsters You Made, listen to the pain and anger in the lyrics, and to Ama Ata Aidoo's spoken words at the end.

werk/cabaret-voltaire-mix-up.text:
Mix-Up is the debut album by the English band Cabaret Voltaire. It was released on 23 October 1979 on the label Rough Trade. The line-up consisted of Stephen Mallinder on vocals, bass and percussion, Chris Watson on synthesizers and tapes, and Richard H. Kirk on guitar, synthesizers and wind instruments, with Haydn Boyes Weston on drums.

The record includes a cover of No Escape, a song by The Seeds from 1966. The first reactions were divided. One reviewer called the album interesting but only rarely appealing, another heard fascinating music that seldom hangs together. Later, Head Heritage wrote that it was a snapshot of a brief period in British post-punk, when bands ventured into a strange, homemade white dub landscape. AllMusic too saw it as an important part of the post-punk of 1978 to 1982.
werk/cabaret-voltaire-mix-up.listen: In No Escape, listen to how this song by The Seeds sounds in the hands of a post-punk band.

werk/cabaret-voltaire-red-mecca.text:
During a tour of the United States in November 1979, Cabaret Voltaire became interested in the rise of the Christian right and its use of television. The band compared that with the growth of Islamic politics in the Middle East. Red Mecca, recorded in May 1981 at Western Works in Sheffield, tied those themes to the bleak atmosphere of impoverished northern England under Margaret Thatcher. Richard H. Kirk pointed to Afghanistan and the American hostages in Iran as the occasion for the title.

The album was released in August 1981 on Rough Trade and reached the top of the British independent albums chart. NME placed it ninth in its year-end list. AllMusic called the record tight and dense, without a single quiet moment. In 2019 Pitchfork counted it among the best industrial albums of all time.
werk/cabaret-voltaire-red-mecca.listen: Listen to A Touch of Evil. Notice the echo and the space in the sound.

werk/cabaret-voltaire-the-voice-of-ameri.text:
Cabaret Voltaire released The Voice of America in July 1980 on Rough Trade. It is the English group's third studio album. The band members recorded and produced it themselves. The record opens with a piece of newsreel of police officers being given instructions on how to deal with Beatles fans, ahead of a Beatles concert in 1966. Stay Out of It contains three sentences from the episode Demon with a Glass Hand of The Outer Limits.

Trouser Press wrote that the new material had far more focus and cleaner production than earlier work. The mantra, the constant repetition of a pattern, replaced the chaotic electronic noise of before. AllMusic found it less spectacular than what was still to come, but not without tension. In Partially Submerged, SF Weekly heard a mixture of Krautrock and free jazz.
werk/cabaret-voltaire-the-voice-of-ameri.listen: Listen to Partially Submerged. Notice the Moog and the way the piece sounds like a mixture of Krautrock and free jazz.

werk/camaron-de-la-isla-al-verte-las-flo.text:
This flamenco album from 1969 is a collaboration between the singer Camarón de la Isla and the guitarist Paco de Lucía. It is one of the first six albums they made together. Officially it was called El Camarón de la Isla con la colaboración especial de Paco de Lucía, but in practice the records were named after their first track, and that is how this one got its title.

The twelve tracks show how many styles exist within flamenco. The form is listed for each track: bulerías, tientos, seguiriyas, fandangos, tarantos, tangos, soleares and alegrías. Paco de Lucía plays guitar, and a second guitar comes from Ramón de Algeciras. The album opens with the bulerías Al verte las flores lloran and closes with the alegrías Barrio de Santa María.
werk/camaron-de-la-isla-al-verte-las-flo.listen: In Si Acaso Muero, a seguiriyas, listen to how the guitar accompanies the singing.

werk/can-can.text:
Can was released in 1979, after the group had broken up, on Harvest in Germany and Laser Records in England. The recording had been made in February 1978 at Inner Space Studios in Weilerswist near Cologne. Holger Czukay now only did the tape editing. The sound is cleaner and more spacious than on the two preceding records. On Safe, Jaki Liebezeit's drums and Rosko Gee's bass fit together more tightly than before.

A Spectacle was written by the group as a signature tune for the ZDF programme Aspekte, and Efs No. 99 Can Can is a wild arrangement of Offenbach's Infernal Galop. Reviewers saw the album as a solid conclusion to the first period. Biographer Rob Young heard a band that sounded far less constrained than on the previous record.
werk/can-can.listen: Listen to Safe and notice the voice, which has been put through a vocoder, and how closely drums and bass work together here.

werk/can-flow-motion.text:
Flow Motion is Can's seventh studio album and was released in October 1976. Recording began in the spring of 1976 at their own Inner Space Studio in Cologne. Since Landed the group had been working with a 16-track machine. As a result the members more often recorded their parts separately, and there were more guitar lines from Michael Karoli and more keyboards from Irmin Schmidt. The lyrics were written by engineer Peter Gilmour.

The group sounded cleaner, more playful and calmer than before and added disco and reggae. I Want More is short, catchy and danceable, reached number 26 on the British chart and brought the band to Top of the Pops. Laugh Till You Cry, Live Till You Die was Can's first reggae song, with Karoli on the Turkish bağlama. Cascade Waltz combines a reggae beat with a waltz. Critics were divided over the record.
werk/can-flow-motion.listen: Listen to Cascade Waltz and notice how a reggae beat and a waltz time can be heard at the same time.

werk/can-future-days.text:
After the tour for Ege Bamyasi, Can first took four weeks' holiday. That sunny mood is in the album. Holger Czukay travelled to Southeast Asia, Damo Suzuki to Japan, Irmin Schmidt to the south of France and Michael Karoli to the Portuguese coast. In the summer of 1973 the group recorded at their own Inner Space Studio in Weilerswist, the most complex production they had done up to then. It was the last album with singer Suzuki.

The music leaves ordinary rock structures behind and uses sounds that spread out widely, with bubbling rhythms and layers of keyboards. The title track begins with a minute of abstract electroacoustic music that grows into a groove. Bel Air was the first track to be recorded, in a single session, and it contains the recording of a bird in a meadow. Biographer Rob Young calls the album the group's most weightless achievement.
werk/can-future-days.listen: In Bel Air, listen to the soft opening with the wind-like sounds and to the birdsong that is worked into the piece.

werk/can-landed.text:
Landed is the sixth studio album by the German Krautrock group Can and was released in September 1975 on Virgin Records. It was recorded at Inner Space Studios in Weilerswist near Cologne, where Holger Czukay led the recording. For the first time the group used a 16-track recorder instead of a two-track machine. This allowed them to layer more sounds, and Czukay spoke of the first professional mix. The title refers to the landing after the previous record, Soon Over Babaluma.

On Red Hot Indians, two sax solos by Olaf Kübler of Amon Düül can be heard. Hunters and Collectors was released as a single in Germany. Critics were divided: one reviewer found the record straightforward, another called it the group's last great one. Irmin Schmidt himself was unhappy with the harsh mix of the A-side.
werk/can-landed.listen: Listen to Red Hot Indians and notice the saxophones, which give the song something strange and tropical.

werk/can-monster-movie.text:
Monster Movie is Can's debut album, released in August 1969 by the small German label Music Factory. A year earlier the group had recorded Prepared to Meet Thy PNOOM, but no record company wanted to release it. Monster Movie was a second, more commercial attempt. It was recorded at Schloss Nörvenich, a fourteenth-century castle. Bassist and engineer Holger Czukay, a former student of Karlheinz Stockhausen, mastered it. Singer Malcolm Mooney sings all the songs.

The album mixes psychedelic rock, blues, free jazz and world music. The influence of The Velvet Underground can be heard above all in Father Cannot Yell. Improvisation, experiment and the editing of recordings became the basis for the later Krautrock sound. The closing track Yoo Doo Right lasts twenty minutes and was edited down from six hours of improvisation. The first pressing of five hundred copies sold out quickly, after which Liberty Records took the album on.
werk/can-monster-movie.listen: Listen to Yoo Doo Right and notice the interplay between organ and drums. A reviewer in 1969 heard Morse code and a machine gun in it.

werk/can-tago-mago.text:
In 1970 bassist Holger Czukay and drummer Jaki Liebezeit saw a street musician playing in front of a cafe in Munich. That evening Damo Suzuki performed with them, and he became Can's new singer. The double album Tago Mago was recorded between November 1970 and February 1971 at Schloss Nörvenich, a medieval castle near Cologne. Czukay worked with just three microphones and two two-track recorders, often sixteen hours a day, and edited the long jams into songs.

The first record is more conventional in design, the second far more experimental. Aumgn and Peking O, with Czukay's tape and radio experiments, make it the group's most extreme record. Miles Davis, Karlheinz Stockhausen and the occultist Aleister Crowley served as inspiration. The manager insisted that the second LP be released as well. The album received broad praise, and Ned Raggett called it one of the best albums ever.
werk/can-tago-mago.listen: In Peking O, listen to the drum machine, an early Ace Tone Rhythm Ace, playing together with acoustic drums.

werk/candy-dulfer-sax-a-go-go.text:
Sax-A-Go-Go is the second album by the Dutch alto saxophonist Candy Dulfer and was released in 1993. On the album she plays alto, tenor, baritone and soprano saxophone. Ulco Bed co-wrote many of the songs and played bass guitar, guitar and drums, among other things. In the United States the album entered the Contemporary Jazz chart in February 1994 at number 5 and stayed there for 31 weeks.

On the title track Dulfer works with Easy Mo Bee. She also plays covers: Compared to What, Eugene McDaniels's protest song against the war in Vietnam, and I Can't Make You Love Me, known from Bonnie Raitt. The album closes with Sunday Afternoon by Prince, which lasts more than eight minutes.
werk/candy-dulfer-sax-a-go-go.listen: Listen to I Can't Make You Love Me and notice how the saxophone takes the place of the singing voice here.

werk/candy-dulfer-saxuality.text:
With this debut album the Dutch alto saxophonist Candy Dulfer made her name internationally. She produced it together with Ulco Bed, who also took care of keyboards, guitars, synth bass and drum programming. The album is mainly instrumental, but Dulfer and Bed also sing along on a few tracks. Frans Hendrix handled the recording and Susan Rogers mixed the album in Los Angeles. Some editions also include the worldwide hit Lily Was Here, with Dave Stewart on guitar.

The album entered the chart in the Netherlands at number 4 and went gold. It also reached the American and British charts and sold more than a million copies worldwide. It received a Grammy nomination for Best Contemporary Jazz Album. To promote the record, Dulfer toured Europe and the United States.
werk/candy-dulfer-saxuality.listen: Listen to Saxuality and notice how the alto saxophone carries the melody while the programming and the keyboards lay the rhythm beneath it.

werk/canned-heat-hallelujah.text:
Hallelujah is Canned Heat's fourth album and was released in 1969. It was the last album of the first line-up, because guitarist Henry Vestine left the group before the next album. Recording took place from January to May 1969 at I. D. Sound Recorders in Hollywood. Skip Taylor and the group produced it together.

The album mixes original songs with covers of blues classics. The song Canned Heat, credited to Robert Hite Jr., actually comes from Tommy Johnson, and Sic 'em Pigs is co-credited to Booker T. White. Alan Wilson sings and plays guitar and harmonica on tracks such as Change My Ways, Time Was and Get Off My Back. Huautla is an instrumental piece by drummer Fito de la Parra, with bongos and congas by Mike Pacheco. The album entered the Billboard chart on 9 August 1969 and reached number 37, staying for fifteen weeks.
werk/canned-heat-hallelujah.listen: Listen to Time Was and notice Alan Wilson's singing and guitar.

werk/canned-heat-living-the-blues.text:
Living the Blues is Canned Heat's third album, a double album released in late 1968. It was one of the first double albums to sell well: the record reached number 18 on the Billboard chart and stayed for seventeen weeks. The first side contains Going Up the Country, the group's best-known song, which was later used in the Woodstock film. Guests included John Mayall on piano and Dr. John on Boogie Music.

The rest of the album is long and experimental. Parthenogenesis is a psychedelic suite of almost twenty minutes, in nine parts. Refried Boogie, recorded live, takes up two whole sides and lasts longer than the suite. Here it becomes clear that the band was at home both in short blues songs and in long jams. The producers were Skip Taylor and the band themselves.
werk/canned-heat-living-the-blues.listen: Listen to Going Up the Country and notice the flute and the light rhythm, which turn an old blues lyric into a cheerful song.

werk/canned-heat-vintage.text:
Vintage is the sixth album by the American blues rock group Canned Heat and was released in 1970. Johnny Otis produced it. The recordings date from 1966, when the group was still called Canned Heat Blues Band. They were demos and also the first time the group played in a studio. They stayed on the shelf for four years.

The repertoire consists mainly of blues classics by Willie Dixon, Tommy Johnson, John Lee Hooker and Muddy Waters, among others. Rollin' and Tumblin' is on it twice, once without and once with Alan Wilson's harmonica. The album entered the Billboard chart on 17 January 1970 and stayed for five weeks, with number 173 as its highest position. The same sessions have since reappeared on many reissues.
werk/canned-heat-vintage.listen: Listen to both versions of Rollin' and Tumblin' and notice what Alan Wilson's harmonica adds.

werk/cannonball-adderley-in-the-land-of-.text:
In the Land of Hi-Fi is a studio album by Sarah Vaughan from 1955. She recorded it from 25 to 27 October in New York, with the orchestra of Ernie Wilkins, who also arranged and conducted. Bob Shad produced. The orchestra includes trombonists Kai Winding and J.J. Johnson, saxophonist Cannonball Adderley, pianist Jimmy Jones and drummer Roy Haynes, among others.

The repertoire consists of twelve standards, including by George and Ira Gershwin, Rodgers and Hart and Duke Ellington. Over the Rainbow opens the record. Cherokee and How High the Moon each last well over two and a half minutes. Alternative takes from these sessions, with a young Adderley, later appeared on The Complete Sarah Vaughan On Mercury, Vol. 1.
werk/cannonball-adderley-in-the-land-of-.listen: Listen to Over the Rainbow and notice how Vaughan's voice relates to Wilkins's orchestra.

werk/cannonball-adderley-somethin-else.text:
Cannonball Adderley recorded this album on 9 March 1958 and released it in August on Blue Note, the only one he made for that label. At the time he was playing in Miles Davis's quintet, shortly after its record Milestones, and Davis took part as trumpeter, one of the few times he recorded as a sideman. Davis plays several of the first solos, wrote the bluesy title track and, according to the sleeve notes, chose most of the material. Hank Jones, Sam Jones and Art Blakey also played, with Alfred Lion as producer.

The trumpeter said that his approach to Autumn Leaves came out of the inspiration of pianist Ahmad Jamal. At the end of One for Daddy O you can hear him ask Lion whether this is what he wanted. DownBeat gave the record five stars in 1958, praising Davis's lyrical playing on Autumn Leaves. The Penguin Guide to Jazz placed the album in its core selection.
werk/cannonball-adderley-somethin-else.listen: In Autumn Leaves, listen to Miles Davis's lyrical trumpet playing, which DownBeat already praised in 1958.

werk/cannonball-adderley-sophisticated-s.text:
Sophisticated Swing is Cannonball Adderley's fifth album and his fourth on EmArcy. He plays here in a quintet with his brother Nat Adderley on cornet, Junior Mance on piano, Sam Jones on bass and Jimmy Cobb on drums. Recording took place at Capitol Studios in New York, on 6, 8 and 11 February 1957. The photograph on the sleeve was taken by Chuck Stewart, at the Ulysses S. Grant Monument in Chicago.

The repertoire consists of original pieces by Nat Adderley, Gene Wright and Sam Jones, among others, along with standards such as Spring Is Here and Stella By Starlight. In AllMusic, Scott Yanow called the music bop-oriented and bluesy, but less soulful than later.
werk/cannonball-adderley-sophisticated-s.listen: Listen to Stella By Starlight and notice the interplay of the alto saxophone with the rhythm section.

werk/carla-bley-dinner-music.text:
Carla Bley recorded Dinner Music in 1976 and it was released in 1977 on the label Watt, in association with ECM. She plays organ, piano and tenor saxophone, and sings. The line-up is large and remarkable: Roswell Rudd on trombone, Bob Stewart on tuba, Richard Tee on piano, Steve Gadd on drums and guitarists Cornell Dupree and Eric Gale, among others.

The record has eight tracks, from Sing Me Softly of the Blues to A New Hymn. Michael G. Nastos of AllMusic called the album a first excursion down a funky path, impeccably executed and almost indispensable. In Dining Alone the lyrics are by Bley and John Hunt.
werk/carla-bley-dinner-music.listen: Listen to Sing Me Softly of the Blues and notice how the rhythm section and the brass together lay down a funky foundation.

werk/carla-bley-sextet.text:
Sextet was released in 1987 on the label Watt/ECM. The album was made with a six-piece group: Carla Bley on organ and synthesizer bass, Larry Willis on piano, Hiram Bullock on guitar, Steve Swallow on bass guitar, Victor Lewis on drums and Don Alias on percussion. All six pieces were written by the bandleader herself. They each last from just over six to just over seven and a half minutes.

The AllMusic reviewer heard a polished, golden sound that suits the ECM style well. The Penguin Guide to Jazz gave the album two and a half stars. It is a calm and carefully made album, made by a small group who give one another space.
werk/carla-bley-sextet.listen: Listen to More Brahms and notice how organ and piano share the space with guitar and bass.

werk/carla-bley-social-studies.text:
Carla Bley recorded Social Studies in 1980. The album was released in 1981 on the label Watt/ECM. She plays organ and piano and leads a large group of wind players: trumpet, saxophones, clarinet, euphonium, trombone and tuba. Steve Swallow plays bass guitar and D. Sharpe drums. The album has six tracks, from almost five to almost thirteen minutes.

The longest track is Reactionary Tango, a piece in three parts that she wrote together with Swallow. Reviewer Alex Henderson called the album adventurous and unconventional, and the Penguin Guide to Jazz wrote that the bookish sleeve conceals wonderfully dry music.
werk/carla-bley-social-studies.listen: Listen to Reactionary Tango and notice how the piece is built in three parts and how the horns take turns.

werk/carla-bley-tropic-appetites.text:
Tropic Appetites was released in 1974, as a follow-up to her debut Escalator over the Hill. The lyrics are by her friend Paul Haines and are about his travels through Southeast Asia in the preceding years. Unlike the orchestral Escalator, the line-up here is an octet, with Julie Tippetts as singer.

The record contains eight pieces, ranging from the short In India, which lasts a little over a minute, to What Will Be Left Between Us and the Moon Tonight? and Song of the Jungle Stream, which both last more than ten minutes. Bley herself plays organ, piano, marimba and much more, and produced the record together with Michael Mantler. The line-up includes Dave Holland on bass and Paul Motian on drums, among others.
werk/carla-bley-tropic-appetites.listen: Listen to What Will Be Left Between Us and the Moon Tonight? and notice Julie Tippetts's voice in Paul Haines's lyrics.
